slides.text: Former grandmaster Victor lived alone in a secluded cottage in Vermont, passing his retirement playing postal chess with an anonymous opponent signed only as 'The Rook.' Every two weeks for three years, a postcard would arrive with a move written in neat blue cursive—14. Nf3, 19. exd5. Victor admired the player’s relentless, suffocating positional strategy. But in the spring of his fourth year, Victor noticed something chilling about the postmarks stamped on the cards.

The first twenty moves had been postmarked from Prague. The next ten were mailed from London, then Montreal, then Boston. Each card was mailed from a city geographically closer to Vermont. Three weeks ago, the postmark was Burlington, forty miles away. Yesterday, the card arrived postmarked from the village post office two miles down his road: 38. Qxd7+. Victor looked at the wooden board on his study table. The move was a brilliant tactical sacrifice that forced his king into a corner with no legal retreat.

Tonight, Victor found an envelope slipped under his front door—with no stamp, no postal mark, and no return address. Hands trembling, he tore it open. Inside was a black chess pawn carved from human bone and a single index card with one final notation written in damp blue ink: '39. Mate in one. Turn off the reading lamp and check behind your curtains.' Victor blew out the lamp, and in the window reflection, saw the shadow standing behind his chair.
